speechtext:
['Mr. Chairman, if any hon. friend will insist upon it, all I have to say is that this statement was made on the 29th of November last when the hon.
member for East Hastings expressed himself strongly in favour of reciprocity. He assured us that he would hold up both hands in favour of such an arrangement.
I would ask my hon. friend from East Hastings if he will put up one hand in favour of it if it comes to a vote now. In case anybody may think I am not quoting him properly I have taken the page and day when he spoke, so that anybody will see what the hon. gentleman said. The same thing is true of the hon. member for East Huron (Mr. Chisholm) who spoke on November 24, 1910, as reported at pages 258 and 263 of ' Hansard."* The same expression of opinion was given by that hon. gentleman. He thought it would be a splendid thing if we could get it. The only thing that was bothering the hon. member for East Huron was how to get it. He was a man of an independent type-put it before us and I will vote for it! That was the opinion of the hon. member for East Huron. I will expect that the hon. gentleman will show this brand of independence and vote for this agreement if it comps to a vote.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have quoted a great many opinions but I have quoted none with greater satisfaction and greater faith than the two last opinions, because, judging from what has been going on around me here for the last three weeks, the fiery eloquence of the hon. member for East Hastings denouncing and condemning this agreement in all the^ moods and tenses, I certainly could not think that he had ever expressed a view in favour of the proposal. Then, having discovered this oasis in the desert, I find there are saints in Caesar's house and that from all quarters we are getting support for this agreement. As I said at the commencement it is getting stronger, and gaining strength as the days go by. I am not going to quote from this Manitoba paper called the ' Tribune,' but I will ask any hon. gentleman to look at it. It is a Winnipeg paper of some repute, I believe, it is dated the 6th March, 1911, and at page 4 hon. gentlemen from Manitoba who are interested no doubt in what is going on in that province, will see resolutions passed at different points in Manitoba by which the legislature is condemned and in which members are condemned to their faces, being present at these meetings, for the course they have taken and told emphatically that they misrepresented the people of Manitoba when they took the course they did take in supporting the resolution introduced by the premier of that province.
That is the condition there, and in so far as the maritime provinces, Quebec, and I think the most part of Ontario outside of', "the centres which are on party grounds against us now we have nothing to fear and everything to hope from this bargain. I have here a paper called ' Farm and Home ' published in Springfield, Massachusetts, and Chicago which has a circulation of over one million copies in the United States, and on its front page is an editorial stating that this agreement is a bad thing for the American farmer and gives the Canadian farmer much the best of it, and certainly if it is a bad thing lor the American farmer according to this newspaper, it must be a good thing for our agricultural community. I now, Sir, have gone over the ground as fully and as rapidly as I could, but I presume my hon. friend (Mr. Bradbury) who follows me will be obliged to take the same course as I did the other night and adjourn the debate. He must excuse me for having taken up so much time, but I can assure my hon. friend that I would like to have concluded at an earlier hour in the evening. I am satisfied, Sir, that upon every ground this is an excellent ap-eement for the people of Canada, that it gives them opportunities which otherwise they could not have, that it is letting us in on the ground floor of the trade of a great country with a population of 100,000,000, a country that every day is needing a greater supply of the products which we can produce, and a country which before many years will possibly be in the same position as England is to-day, importing enormous quantities of food stuffs while exporting none, and devoting itself entirely to its great manufacturing industries. ' If that should come to pass, and if Canada for many years to come will be a produceir of such commodities as will be required for the supply of this industrial nation to the south, is it not well that we should get in now, and hold that market and develop it, rather than that we should let the opportunity slip, and give a chance to other countries to occupy the field against us. We are told that Argentine grows the same kind of natural products as we do, and is our competitor, and is it not in our interest to see that the Argentine Republic does not get a foothold in the United States market ahead of us. Would it not be a good thing for us to hold that market as against all the world? I can see no ground on which we have anything to fear or anything to lose, but I can see on the other hand that we have everything to gain. Then, so far as our loyalty is concerned I hardly think it is worth while discussing it at all. As I pointed out the other evening, where are they going to find the traitors, where are they going to find the man who will not be true to the British flag? We are getting too old in this country to cast off our allegiance; we are proud of our flag, we are proud of the history and tradi-Mr. McKENZIE.
tions of our country, proud of our institutions, proud of being Britishers. What consolation would I or any other Canadian feel in throwing up our caps on the 4th of July? Surely it would take us a long time to get trained to that. We will not try it, and the American people know better than to try to put that yoke over us. We are willing to trade with them, we are willing to develop with them, we are willing to take advantage of the growth and prosperity that would come to us by reason of that trade, but we shall always be true to Canada, true to our own flag, proud of being part and parcel of the greatest empire the world has even seen, an empire on which the sun never sets. I do not think it is worthy of this parliament to discuss such a question as whether or not we will remain true to our own country. We certainly shall. But, while being true to the British Empire we are also as sensible business men bound to take advantage of every trade opportunity that presents itself to make this a great country commercially, and, Sir, as Canada grows in strength, so grows the strength and the standing of the British Empire.
Mr. BRADBURY moved that the committee rise."]

McKENZIE (North Cape Breton)	resuming-Mr. Chairman, when I moved the adjournment of the debate on Thursday night last, I was discussing the attitude of the different political parties in Canada towards the coal industry. It is well known that in Ontario and in the western sections of Canada fault is found with the Canadian plenipotentiaries particularly with the Minister of Finance that he did not reduce the coal duty more than he did, while the Conservative press in Nova Scotia and in the east, find fault with him because he reduced that tariff too much, and the argument is there made by our Conservative friends that the Liberal government and the Liberal party are not the friends of that great industry. In this way is capital sought to be made against the government. I was pointing out, Sir, when the debate was adjourned, that on every occasion when the coal industry of Nova Scotia required consideration and protection it received that consideration and

protection from the Minister of Finance and from this government. I was pointing out further that the Conservative party had no claim to any particular guardianship over that great industry and that their history does not give them any warrant to claim that they have done anything in particular for the coal industry in Canada, and particularly in Nova Scotia, where the industry really had its origin. It is contended by members of the Conservative party that the National Policy was largely created originally for the sake of the coal industry and that it has done it much good. But, I would point out that practically throughout the whole life of the National Policy there was a statutory offer that coal would be made free of 'duty in Canada whenever it was made free of duty in the United States, an offer which stood on the statute-books of Canada from 1879 down to 1904, two years before the Conservatives went out of office. That offer was allowed to stand on our statute-books for 16 years by the Conservatives, and no advantage having been taken of it, I suppose they got tired of seeing it there and so they took it off. I also pointed out that in 1890 the Right Hon. Sir John Macdonald then Prime Minister of Canada offered free coal to the United States. Now, I do not think there is any responsible person in this House on the Conservative side who will say that coal should be protected to any greater extent than it will be under this compact if ratified, or protected to any greater extent than it is by the tariff as it stands to-day. When I had the honour of holding a seat in the legislature of Nova Scotia this question of duty on coal was under consideration. As the members who represent the coal counties of Nova Scotia are called to task for their support of this government, and as my own course in that regard is called in question, I wish to point out that the position I am taking to-day on the coal question, is but the position I have always taken. Speaking in the local House over ten years ago, as may be found on page 7 of the Debates of trie Legislature of Nova Scotia for the year 1901, I said: I
I am in favour of duties upon coal, and of bounties upon iron and steel and of everything that is considered to be necessary for the protection of every industry now established or hereafter to be established in the province of Nova Scotia or in the Dominion.
It is not necessary for me to quote anything further from the address I made to the legislature at that time. The short quotation which I have made shows the position which I then took, a position which I still occupy. I submit, therefore, *that it is not fair for hon. gentlemen 166
either in this House or out of it to be claiming for themselves a position in regard to that great industry, in the province of Nova Scotia, in British Columbia, or wherever we have mining coal, to whicri they are not entitled. It is said in the press of Nova Scotia that the Premier of that province, the Hon. G. H. Murray, is not favourable to the coal industry, and that he is in the compact with those who are making the agreement with the United States to ruin the coal industry. The Hon. Mr. Murray has a record on the coal question that puts him beyond any attacks of that kind. When there was some speculation in 1897, when it was not known what the Fielding tariff was going to be in regard to the duties on coal, the Premier of Nova Scotia dissolved the legislature, called upon the people to pass judgment on that question, and nailed his colours to the mast in favour of a tariff sufficient to protect that great industry. The Hon. Mr. Murray, having taken that position at that time and every time since, has made a record for himself that will not bear any adverse criticism to-day from I on. gentlemen who may wish to make political capital out of the slight reduction in the coal duty now proposed.
So far as the present agreement is concerned, I have heard no specific criticism of it from hon. gentlemen on the opposition side. They make the bald statement that it is a bad agreement, that it is going to disturb conditions in this country, that it is a severe blow at the loyalty of the people of this country. But there is no specific criticism of any particular item of the agreement. Nobody has said, here is something that should be in the agreement that is left out, or here is something in it that should not be there. I have heard no gentleman of responsibility, or indeed no member of this House, telling the Minister of Finance that he has not_dealt with the coal industry or the steel industry in the best interest of those industries; and while the hon. gentleman who is responsible for the policy and the destinies of the Conservative party in this House does not venture to say anything against the agreement so far as these industries are concerned, I submit that the press and others outside of this House who speak on the side of that party are stopped from taking that ground. On the question of the tariff generally, the position of the Conservative party is most extraordinary. In 1897, when the Fielding tariff was brought down, Sir Chas. Tapper assailed it on the ground that it was to be the ruin. of every industry, every mine and every other work that, according to him, depended for its existence upon the tariff policy of the' Conservative party. This chorus was taken

1878 to 1896, the country made less progress during that period on the average than it was making up to the time of the inauguration of the National Policy. Giving the figures exactly as they appear upon the blue-book from 1868 to 1878 the increase in trade in that ten year period was $44,175,823, or an average increase per year of $4,417,582. During the period of 18 years when our hon. friends opposite were in power, from 1878 to 1896, the total increase was $66,000,000, making an annual increase of $3,666,666, or about a million dollars less per year during that 18 years than during the ten year period following confederation. That is the record which my hon. friend would have to show if he had confined his calculation to the period when his friends were in power. From 1896 to 1910, the proud period of the regime of my right hon. friend and those he has gathered around him, the increase was $457,000,000, making an average increase per year of not $3,000,000, not $4,000,000, nor four times that, but of $326,-365,711. That is a record of_ increase of which the government, the friends of the government, and the country have reason to be proud and satisfied. But, I do not think the leader of the opposition would be [DOT]satisfied with the advance that was^ made by the country under the regime of his own friends. But if you lump the whole sum, if you put it altogether it makes a good -showing and gives him a better opportunity of saying:	Let well enough alone. I do
not think in all seriousness that the leader of the opposition is sufficiently ambitious for his party or his country when he asks -as, under present conditions, to let well 'enough alone. The whole country may be making fair progress, but I must say that -while I am fairly proud of the conditions In the maritime provinces, and the growth that is going on there, I do not think we have any reason to be satisfied with the progress we are making, and I submit without any hesitation that the progress which is being made in the maritime provinces today is n6t well enough compared with other parts of the country. Within the: last * twenty years we have lost three of our representatives in this House. We have three [DOT]members less from Nova Scotia to-day than we had when the population began to go down, or at least when we were unable to hold our own with the rest of the Dominion. New Brunswick and Prince Edward 'Island have lost members, and, therefore, I submit that the leader of the opposition lias no right to say that we in the maritime provinces- should sit down and say that we are content with the present conditions when we are not holding our own with the *rest of Canada. We have a Tight to expect assistance from that hon. gentleman, and when he has reason to believe, as he has, 'Siat this agreement would help to build up Mr. McKENZIE.
our population,, that it would aid our fishing industry, mining, farming and everything else and give an impetus to our prosperity .as reciprocity did before, that we would hold our representation in parliament, that we would hold our end up better under this arrangement than we do now, he has no warrant to say to the people of the maritime provinces to leave well enough alone, and not put forward an effort to better their condition.
I submit, Sir, talking not very seriously, that if the leader of the opposition wants to apply that doctrine to his own job, to his own position in this country, we have no objection from the Liberal standpoint as far as my hon. friend being leader of the opposition is concerned, because we are quite content to let well enough alone, and to let him occupy his present position, but we are not satisfied to let him apply that doctrine to the trade, commerce and general prosperity of the country. If it comes to that I think my hon. friend should amend his motto and say:	What we have, we 11
hold, and what we have not we are after. That is what I think would suit us better in the maritime provinces, _and generally all over this country. It will not be contended, Sir, in this tremendously large, prosperous and wealthy country that we occupv-wealthy iu natural resources, in area and extent-that we can afford to let well enough alone with a population of only 8,000,000 at the outset when we have a territory capable of supporting a population as large as _ that which the same area is supporting on the other side of the line. Is it not , our duty not to be contented with the growth we are making, but to move along as rapidly as possible, and to build up this country so that without any undue delay we may be benefiting our people side by side with those of the great nation to the -south of us, and placing them in a position of equality in every line of life.
I was going to say something more about the figures quoted by the leader of the opposition and those of other gentlemen, but after all his speech and the speech of the hon. member for North io-ronto (Mr. Foster) are the keynotes to the speeches made by hon. gentlemen on that side of the House. What did the leader of the opposition say in giving evidence of the prosperity of this country? He said that all we had to do was to look at the speeches of the Minister of Finance in support of the budget for the last fourteen years, and we would see evidences of the great prosperity of this country. So that there should be no mistake about where I am quoting the hon. gentleman, this was on the 7th February, and it appears at page 3366 of ' Hansard.' We were invited to look at the history of the budget of the

Liberal party for the last fourteen years for evidences of the prosperity of this country.
It is quite true-in what possibly, from a party standpoint, might be regarded as a moment of weakness in the tactics of the leader of the opposition-that he refers us to the history not of his own party but to the history of the Liberal party. And what is the record that the leader of the opposition invites us to study? It is a proud record for this country and a proud record for the Minister of Finance. Practically the_ first year the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) was in power he announced a surplus of $1,722,112.33; the next year he announced a surplus of $4,837,149, the next year a surplus of $8,054,714, the next year a surplus of $5,648,333, the next year a surplus of $7,291,388, the next year a surplus of $14,345,166, the next year a surplus of $15,056,984, the next year a. surplus of $7,863,099, the next year a surplus of $12,898,719, the next year a surplus of $16,427,167, the next year a surplus of $19,413,054, the next year a surplus of $1,029,171.97 and the last year for which we have a record a surplus of $22,091,184.47. That is the record to which the leader of the opposition invites us to inquire for evidence of the prosperity of this country. The hon. gentleman took care not to refer us to the records of his own party because there we find deficits and not surpluses. In 1885 the Conservative government had to announce a deficit of $2,240,058, in 1886 a deficit of $5,834,571.87, in 1888 a deficit of $810,031.26, in 1893 a deficit of $1,210,332.45, in 1894 a deficit of $4,153,875.58, in 1896 a deficit of $330,551.31. That, Sir, is the record that was presented to us by the budgets of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) when he was Minister of Finance. I suppose it was quite right for the leader of the opposition to refer us to the speeches of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) for evidences of prosperity, and it is only fair that the people of this country should know what that record is as compared with the record of the Conservative party when they controlled the finances of Canada.
Without breaking away from this subject I come to say a word on the question of the authority of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs to make this arrangement. I hold that when the Liberal party submitted their programme to the country in 1893 and told the people categorically what they intended to do and the subjects with which they would deal if they were placed in power and the Conservatives turned out, then when the people of the country placed Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier's government in office with a knowledge of the things they promised to do I submit that until that programme is exhausted and everything promised by the leaders of the Liberal party carried into effect this government has a mandate from the people with respect to every plank in their platform of 1893. I do not think there is anything illogical in that; I think it is a position that can be sustained before any jury in this country. I would not hesitate to submit to the electors of any county in Canada, that the Liberal government having had a mandate from the people to carry into effect every item in their programme when they came to power, the Liberal party has a perfect right to go on without any further mandate. Our friends of the opposition profess to be very logical in their reasoning and argument and they often say to the leader of the government: Why dont you carry out your promise to reform the Senate for which you have a mandate from the people. Surely if the Liberal party had a mandate in 1896 to reform the Senate on the platform of 1893, it has a mandate to make a trade agreement with the United States because the two propositions were submitted to the people at one and the same time. If our Conservative friends are consistent and logical in saying that the government have a mandate to reform the Senate, wherein lies the strength of their argument that the government have no mandate to carry out a trade agreement with the United States? For my own part I confess I am not very much concerned whether they have that mandate or not. If this is a good agreement, if this is in the best interests of the Canadian people, if it is calculated to develop trade, if it brings about more friendly relations between this country and the United States I am not concerned very much about whether there is a very full mandate given or not. I submit that we have the power as representatives of the people to do everything which in our judgment is for the best interests of the people, and if this is a good agreement in the best interests of the people that is the only thing I am particularly concerned about. And, Sir, I am satisfied that as time goes on, as day by day this question iis discussed in this House and in the provincial legislatures and in the newspapers and on the hustings, the people will better understand this question and so, day by day the policy of the government will become more popular. I be-live, Sir, that if the people of Canada were to-day called upon to pass judgment on this agreement an overwhelming majority of them would decide in its favour. While, it is not necessary for me at this stage to trace the history of the eflort of the Canadian people to obtain better trade relations with the United States, it is possibly encumbent upon me to point out that the Conservative party as well as the

Liberal party have always been advocating better trade arrangements with the neighbouring republic. I have here a quotation from the first budget speech of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) in this House, as found in ' Hansard ' at page 449, volume I of ' Hansard ' of 1889. On that occasion he had reason to refer to the question of trade relations with the United States, and he said:
The government is ready and willing to co.ne to the aid of the country now and implement to the best of its ability this desire whicn is growing and stretching out from the true and solid basis of trade prosperity at home, in a foreign trade with other countries, so that we may compete with foreign countries in the different wares that we make and the different products that we raise. This country and this government has always been desirous of extending its trade to foreign countries. In all honesty and candour that can be maintained and it cannot be denied. No matter what government has been on the Treasury benches, no matter what party has been in power, there has been a continuous and a persistent attempt to cultivate better trade relations between this country and the United States of America in a reciprocity that should be fair and equally beneficial to both countries. The negotiations of 18G6, of 1869, of 1871, and of 1888, all bear testimony to that. But, Sir, if the country to the south of us will not go upon the lines of the late reciprocity treaty, if it will not trade upon lines which are fair and equal to both countries, and if it continues to show, as it has done in the Senate Bill, and as it has in the President's message, delivered only yesterday, its reiterated adherence to the high and strong protective system that it has placed about its trade-then, Sir, it becomes this country to build upon its own foundations, to develop its own vast natural resources, and to further strengthen the internal industries of the country which will enable her to extend her trade into other countries.
The hon. member for North Toronto, the then Minister of Finance, said that the Conservative government were ready and willing, always ready and willing to make trade arrangements with the United States, but if they could not do so, it was their duty to make trade arrangements with other countries. We hear a great deal to-day about looking to Great Britain and to Great Britain only; but if you look at the speech of the hon. member for North Toronto on that occasion, you will find that the other countries which he mentions do not include Great Britain. They were South America, the West Indies, China, Japan, the islands of the South Pacific, New Zealand and Australia-not a word about Great Britain or about any effort to bring about better trade relations with Great Britain. From the same volume, at page 478, I take a quotation from no less a person than Sir Charles Tupper in sup-Mr. McKENZIE.
port of better trade relations with the United States; and what he says in this:
But no matter how they may endeavour to confuse the public mind, the people understand that the Liberal-Conservative party, as a whole, are still ready to make a fair trade arrangement with the United States, whenever the United States are. prepared to enter into such an arrangement. We have said, time and time again, to .Jhe government at Washington; we have said it in all the official correspondence as these gentlemen themselves admit, our plenipotentiaries have said it; and true to that policy, we are not taking an attitude unworthy of Canadians, we are not taking a cringing attitude. I believe we will yet succeed in making a fair arrangement with the Republican government lately installed at Washington, and we will do it as men and as Canadians, just as independent in Canada in reference to our future and our present as the Americans to their credit, are independent in the United States.
On another occasion, in 1888, at page 674 of volume I -of ' Hansard,' of that year, Sir Charles Tupper said:
I may say that I took the opportunity, when delivering my speech on the financial condition of the country a year ago, to draw the attention of the House to the results of that treaty, and I will just call the attention of the House again one moment to a single extract in that speech, in which I referred to the trade results of what is known as the reciprocity treaty of 1851. It will be found that the United States during those twelve years, from 1854 to 1866, exported to British North America home products to the extent of $300,808,370 and foreign products to the extent of $62,379,718, the total exports to British North America being $363,188,088. The imports from the British provinces into the United States during that period amounted to $267,612,131, showing a balance during the twelve years in favour of the United States of $95,575,975. That is to say, that they sent under the operation of that treaty into the British North American provinces over $95,000,000 more than we sent into that country. I have often been at a loss to know how any person in the United States, and much less how any person in Canada could disparage that treaty, or could speak of it. as a onesided treaty, altogether in favour of British North America, and not equally in favour of the United States. I noticed, shortly aftey the delivery of the speech, that the Hon. T. F. Bayard, the Secretary of State of the United States, was interviewed in relation to this question, and, so far as the account of that interview went, I understood him to confirm the accuracy of the figures which I had used on that occasion. I say I have been greatly at a loss to know how, under the circumstances, any person can be found, especially in this country, to treat this as a onesided measure in the interests of Canada. So far as what is known as Canada is concerned, we know that the trade of our country took a very great bound, and that the result of the reciprocity treaty was to give a very sudden and great and steadily continued impetus to our trade with the United States;

but, as 1 said before, the result was to give ] a still greater expansion of trade to the United* States in relation to British North America. I am glad, after spending some three months in Washington, to be able to say that I had very intimate intercourse with gentlemen of different politics holding high positions in the Senate and House of Representatives, that I took many opportunities of discussing this question with them, and that the result is that I did not find one statesman in the United States who expressed his satisfaction with the termination of that treaty. I believe the general expression in that country is that commercially it was a mistake to have terminated that treaty, and that it would have been infinitely better for the United States and for Canada if it had been continued. As I said before, and as I said the other day, I feel it is only right, in passing, to say, that the effort to obtain the freest possible commercial intercourse between Canada and the United States, consistent with the rights and interests of the two governments, is a policy that does not belong to one party alone, but it is the property of both parties in this country. The hon. member for East York showed his hearty appreciation of the value of such a policy, when he was leading his administration, just as much as my right hon. friend showed it on the occasion of going to Washington in 1871, and on all and every occasion when that question has come up for consideration.
I have several otheT quotations right in line with those, and I submit that if trade relations with the United States were very desirable then, they are equally desirable now. But coming down closer to the present day, since we have been told that what happened in 1888, 1889 and 1903 is ancient history, let me show what stand the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) toi k last fall when discussing the trade question in a magazine published in this country. He was then quite aware that negotiations were going on between Canada and the United States; he was quite familiar with the conditions, and could not have been ignorant of the effect his words would have. Do we find him taking any objection to trade relations with the United States in December, 1910? Talking apparently to some representative of the United States, he said:
We owe you much, we admire your enterprise and your wonderful growth, and sympathize with the efforts you are making to grow rightly and develop the best forces of a great democracy. We covet your virtues and try to avoid your faults, individual, municipal and national. If we can make easier channels for trade between the two countries, consistently with the above conditions, we will be glad to co-operate. Meanwhile, as a neighbourly beginning could you not give our products tariff entrance to your market at the same rates which we accord to yours in our markets? You are bigger, older, richer, more skilled, and more populous. What competition should you fear on a basis of equivalent tariffs? If you were to do this it would be
an earnest of good feeling and might dispose us to further converse.
That was the position taken by the hon. gentleman last December. If he then thought that, subject to the conditions he mentioned-all of which are conserved in this agreement-that it was a good thing to negotiate a trade treaty with the United States, surely nothing has happened since to make it so disastrous as he would now make us believe it is. A few weeks after, I cut a clipping from the speech made by the same hon. gentleman in this House, *and I shall read it to show the tremendous contrast between the two deliverances. In the one I have just Tead, he talks in a very friendly way to this representative of the United States about trade relations. But in the speech he made in this House, he said:
They are coming to the parting of the ways. Who? Canada. What ways? One the bread highway that we began to construct in 1867 running transversely across this continent with its east and west lines and ending, for our markets, in the grand old mother country, the emporium of the markets of the world. And what is the other way? It is the way brushed out and trailed by Messrs. Paterson and Fielding, leading off this old and well-beaten highway down amongst unknown obscurities and hazards, but ending in the United States of America. These are the two ways; and we are at the parting of the ways, says President Taft, and something must be done.
You would imagine that reciprocity was the broad way which leadeth to destruction in its most dreadful form and. that the opposite policy is the narrow way which leads to life everlasting. The trouble however, is that my hon. friend is influenced solely by party politics in his last deliveries. In the first instance, he was evidently speaking his mind without prejudice, when he did not expect such an excellent understanding to be arrived at and was off his guard. He .evidently then did not anticipate that the plenipotentiaries of Canada would obtain such an excellent agreement as they did, and, therefore, was taken off his guard and without having any party consideration before his mind. In the other case he was simply trying to make party capital. In the first instance he was showing what is best in the ^interests of the country so far as trade relations are concerned, but in the other he said the country was going to the dogs, and was trying to lead the people to believe that this policy of the government was a Tuinous one.
I have read sufficient quotations from Sir Charles Tupper and the hon. member for North Toronto to show you what their minds were on this question. But what did the right hon. Sir John Macdonald, when he was leader of the government say:

We said to the Americans, we are perfectly willing to deal with you upon equal terms. We are desirous of having a fair reciprocity treaty, hut we will not consent to open our markets to you whilst yours remain closed to us.
It is perfectly clear from all those extracts, that every one of the great leaders of the Conservative party was for reciprocity with the United States. As a climax to all this, let me quote the words of the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) delivered on the 26th of January last. What did he say, page 2555 of ' Hansard:'
The Conservative party stands to-day, as it has always stood in the past, for the policy of reciprocity within this great British Empire.
Where can* you find in the past of the Conservative party any evidence of this? If the Conservative party had any past, surely that will be found in the speeches of those excellent gentlemen I have quoted and I challenge any one to find anything in that past to show that that party ever stood for reciprocity within the British Empire.
Such a policy was not known and has no well founded existence. As was pointed out by a gentleman in Manitoba the other day, it is the ghost of a corpse buried in Britain at the last general election. That was the language used by a gentleman named Scallion, who is the president of the Grain Growers Association of Manitoba.
I submit, Sir, that there is no such policy, as a practical matter under present conditions, as reciprocity within the empire. A bargain can be made only when two or more parties are willing to enter into it. It is impossible for us to make any trade agreement with the British Empire while the British Empire does not want to enter into .any trade agreement with us that will suit our conditions. Therefore, I submit, this free trade or reciprbcity within the empire is not within the pale of practical politics, and that the people of this country would not be well advised to sit down and twirl their thumbs waiting until the river flowed by or until we could get reciprocity within the empire.
There are many considerations in connection with this agreement which we should take under advisement other than the mere question of dollars and cents. Let me quote the opinion given by so distinguished an American as ex-President Roosevelt:
I feel that we are to be congratulated as a nation upon the likelihood of obtaining a closer reciprocity of tariff and trade relations with Canada. Among all the powers of the earth there is none with which we should desire to be upon more intimate footing of equal rights, to which we should be more closely bound in relations of mutual helpfulness, esteem and good will than in the case of our great neighbour to the north, whose Mr. McKenzie.
prosperity and growth should be a matter of pride to all who dwell on the American continent. I welcome the proposed reciprocity treaty as marking a signal advance in bringing about the closest and most friendly relations between the two countries.
It is no small matter for Canada to get an opinion of that kind from so distinguished a statesman as the ex-President of the United States. I could quote the opinion of the present President and other distinguished men in the United States, if I thought it advisable to do so. I have opinion upon opinion here from the newspapers of Great Britain scouting this idea of disloyalty being involved in this trade agreement. I have already quoted the opinion of Mr. Bryce, the plenipotentiary of Great Britain at Washington, to show that he does not take any stock in that doctrine. I could quote from such 'a strong English paper as the Manchester 1 Guardian ' and other papers of that standing in England that this idea has no justification. Let me quote a few words from an editorial utterance of the London ' Times.' The following appeared in that great newspaper on the 7th of March:
We cannot tell how far the sporadically raised cry of annexation is influencing Canadian opinion, but there is no reason to suppose that the reciprocity agreement would produce any tendency in that direction. On Ithe contrary, bargaining on equal terms with the States might tend to foster rather than diminish the self, reliance and independence of the Canadian people.
That, in short, is about the substance of the opinion of the different English papers as far as I have been able to follow them. We are told that the Americans have no purpose in this arrangement except annexation. A Mr. Bennet moved certain annexation resolutions in Congress. And here is a quotation, from so reputable a paper as the New York ' Times.' I do not know the ' Times' ' politics, but this is, I think, a fair expression of American opinion on the conduct of Mr. Bennet:
(Mr. William S. Bennet, who for a little more than a fortnight longer will represent the Seventeenth New York District in Congress and then retire to private life, has thoroughly justified his defeat at the last election. The impertinent resolution requesting the President to begin negotiations for the annexation of Canada, which he shamelessly introduced Thursday, is an example of a kind of politics that would not astonish anybody if, say, Mr. Macon of Arkansas was the offender. Mr. Bennet, who has hitherto posed as a man of serious character, an energetic if somewhat juvenile statesman looking ti the welfare of his country, has fairly put himself in the blatherskite class. A fine ending to his public career this solicitous friend and supposed confidant of Governor Hughes has made!
The resolution was offered only to be rejected. Its sole purpose is to cause trouble in England and Canada. Probably some of the
,5281

English newspapers which have been opposing Canadian reciprocity will point out that Mr. Bennet's record, until lately, has been fairly good, and that he has won some sort of repute for ability^. He has permitted himself to be used as a catspaw. The reciprocity agreement will prevail in spite of a thousand Rennets. Intelligent Englishmen understand the Bennet kind of politics. There is plenty of the same sort of things in parliament. The measure cannot be beaten in Canada. All the mischief it can accomplish has already been accomplished, and that is not worth worrying about. The voters of the Seventeenth District who elected Mr. Henry George to Congress in November will congratulate themselves on their judgment and foresight.
That is the position taken by the United States on this question, and that was their appreciation of the conduct of this cheap upstart who tried to make trouble in both countries by moving that resolution. I am not going to say that we have any such people in this country, but I think we have people in this House who are making opposition to this agreement that the facts of history will not justify. I hate to weary the House, but I have one quotation more, and it is so important and so directly to the point that I feel obliged to put it on * Hansard.' This is from the Winnipeg ' Free Press,' a newspaper which is supposed to be owned and controlled by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Siftoij). This article appeared in the Winnipeg ' Free Press ' the next day after the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sifton) made his celebrated utterance in this House on the 28th of February last. This is what the paper says, and the people can decide for themselves whether the points are well taken or noj;:
This is a free country and every citizen has a right to make himself beard* when a departure, such as is involved in the acceptance of the reciprocity agreement, is proposed. Nevertheless there are grounds for wondering whether some of the principal objectors have calculated all the possible consequences of the action. Without doubt there is a very considerable volume of independent and disinterested opposition to the agreement. A blind man can see that the agitation to a large degree is not spontaneous. It is being planned, nursed, stage managed, financed and advertised. Who are the men on the job? First, of course, the leaders of the Conservative party who, living up to the full opportunities of their positions are there opposing the government with all the resources at their command. The Toronto machinery of the party is an adept at forming raging and tearing propagandas. Kindly recall the Dundonald affair, the school question and the naval controversy. Each of these agitations started off at a terriffic clip with the 'News' and the 'Telegram' pounding on the big war drums and working up the marching posts to a frenzy. They mostly petered out, it will be recalled, and nobody was a bit worse for all the terriffic cursing in which Brer Willison indulged. If the Toronto Conservatives think this the time and opportunity for another spasm let them have it, as possibly they need one so often to
relieve the pressxire. But it is quite clear that party heat is being powerfully supplemented. Behind this agitation, which starting in Toronto, is involving the industrial and commercial centre of Ontario and is acting and reacting all over Canada, are others and more effective powers. Beyond doubt organized and powerful business interests have thrown the full weight of their enormous influence into the fray to prevent, if possible, the ratification of the agreement. The interests are not difficult to identify. They are chiefly the manufacturers of Ontario. Scratch a manufacturer and you find almost invariably an inveterate foe of reciprocity.
That is the position of the paper said to be owned and controlled by the hon. member for Brandon. I think we can well say that this paper expresses the opinion of the province of Manitoba fairly well. I have here another resolution passed in Manitoba the other day.

He has given his full adhesion to this agreement and has declared himself absolutely opposed to the tactics of the Manitoba legislature and every other machinery put in motion against this contract. I submit that the opinion of Mr. Scallion and of the Grain Growers' Association as represented by Mr. Henders and the other opinions we have seen in the press give us full evidence and full assurance that if any gentleman from Manitoba speaks in this House against this resolution he is not representing the mind of the great province of Manitoba or of the great interests of that province. Now passing through the province of Manitoba I will deal with the resolution that *as before the House in Saskatchewan the other day. I am sure it must have been a startling revelation to our Conservative friends to find so prominent a man as the leader of the opposition of the legislature of that great province coming out fearlessly and openly and declaring himself in favour of this compact. I was in this House in 1905 when there was a great controversy in the west and the great leader in the Conservative party then was Mr. Haultain. He was held up as a great man, but I presume he is no less great a man to-day than he was held to be by the Conservative party in this House when we were asked to follow his lead and take his opinion on the great question in the west in 1905. If he was such a leader then I presume our Conservative friends will be prepared to accept his opinion today. I submit that there is not a man in either of the western provinces who has had a better training in political matters than this hon. gentleman. He was premier of the Northwest Territories for a great number of years and had an opportunity of studying conditions in that country. There is nothing as far as I know or can judge to indicate that he had any other reason in the world for breaking with his party on this subject. I suppose that everything would be the other way. He was the leader of a great party in a great province, and if he had the right end of it by standing by his leaders in this House and in the country I should certainly suppose he would stand by his party. I submit that the evidence is that in coming out in support of this policy he has given his best judgment to what he conceives to be the best interests of his people. In conclusion Mr. Haultain said:
We out here are just as able as the magnates in the east to decide what is patriotic and unpatriotic. I am not prepared to sit at the feet of any of these eastern Gamaliels and study loyalty.
Mr. McKenzie.	.
But that is a sweeping indictment by so able a gentleman as the leader of the opposition in Saskatchewan. He is not going to sit at the feet of Gamaliel Borden, Gamaliel Foster or Gamaliel Whitney or any other Gamaliel from the east; he is prepared to take his own course. He would not even follow the lead of our hon. friend Gamaliel Maclean, who has been addressing the House. I suppose he would put him in the same pot as the other Gamaliels and pursue his own course. I am satisfied that so far as the west is concerned we have the judgment and opinion of as good a man as can be put on the stand in favour of this agreement and against those who for party purposes are opposing it.
I received from a member for the west this afternoon some evidence that seems to me very striking. In the great province of Saskatchewan they have 51 members, local and dominion. I am told, Sir, on the authority of an hon. member from that province that out of 51 there is only one man who is opposing this contract. That one man is the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake) in this House. All the rest are in favour of the agreement. That would look as if, should we accept the challenge that is often thrown out to go before the country, that there is at least one province in which we are sure of a very fair majority because there is in that province only one of those who is elected who dare express an opinion against this agreement.
I do not think that there is veTy much more I should say in support of this proposal. I have pointed out that everything in the contract which I have read is in favour of the Canadian people and in favour of fair mutual trade relations between the two countries.

speechtext:
I am afraid the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) falls sometimes into the habit of quoting evidence that he is not sure of. I am not going to quote any evidence from British Columbia because I do not happen to have any. I am satisfied to let men speak for British Columbia who know that province better than I do. On general principles I believe that British Columbia is all right. British Columbia is an immense lumbering country and I cannot understand why this arrangement would not be good for that industry. British Columbia is a great coal country and I cannot understand why an arrangement of this kind would not be good for the coal industry. I do not think any man should be called upon to stand for the condition of forcing a trade or industry in a country for which it is not adapted. If there is any condition in British Colum-
*5285

bia which is not suitable to fruit raising, if the conditions are such that a man should give his attention..to something else, or put his capital to better use, I am not going to condemn this agreement because it would perhaps strike a forced situation of that kind, but I say that any industry carried on under conditions that are natural to Canada, that are not forced, should be "suited and assisted by this trade agreement. I hope that the fruit growers of British Columbia will have very much better success in connection with this bargain than they think. If they are trying to raise fruit where they should be raising barley, wheat or cattle, I do not think that they should find any fault if they are obliged to abandon that and go into something that is suited to the province of British Columbia and in which they may have better fortune. I hope their fears will not be realized, and I cannot see any reason why the opening up of a market [DOT]of 90,000,000 or a 100,000,000 people should not put them on a better footing than if they have a market of only 8,000,000 people and a very small part of that 8,000,000 people within range of their trade.
Now, there are some other opinions about this agreement which I wish to quote. These are quotations of hon. members holding seats in this House, and I am afraid that the opinions which these hon. gentlemen have recently expressed haVe not been consistent with those which they expressed at an earlier stage in the session. I quote here an opinion which will be found in ' Hansard ', page 408, 29th of November, 1910. It is the opinion of the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) given while speaking in the debate on the address. He is taking the address paragraph by paragraph and he takes this paragraph:
An arrangement may be made which will admit many of the products of the United States in on satisfactory terms.

Mr. Chairman, if any hon. friend will insist upon it, all I have to say is that this statement was made on the 29th of November last when the hon.
member for East Hastings expressed himself strongly in favour of reciprocity. He assured us that he would hold up both hands in favour of such an arrangement.
I would ask my hon. friend from East Hastings if he will put up one hand in favour of it if it comes to a vote now. In case anybody may think I am not quoting him properly I have taken the page and day when he spoke, so that anybody will see what the hon. gentleman said. The same thing is true of the hon. member for East Huron (Mr. Chisholm) who spoke on November 24, 1910, as reported at pages 258 and 263 of ' Hansard."* The same expression of opinion was given by that hon. gentleman. He thought it would be a splendid thing if we could get it. The only thing that was bothering the hon. member for East Huron was how to get it. He was a man of an independent type-put it before us and I will vote for it! That was the opinion of the hon. member for East Huron. I will expect that the hon. gentleman will show this brand of independence and vote for this agreement if it comps to a vote.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I have quoted a great many opinions but I have quoted none with greater satisfaction and greater faith than the two last opinions, because, judging from what has been going on around me here for the last three weeks, the fiery eloquence of the hon. member for East Hastings denouncing and condemning this agreement in all the^ moods and tenses, I certainly could not think that he had ever expressed a view in favour of the proposal. Then, having discovered this oasis in the desert, I find there are saints in Caesar's house and that from all quarters we are getting support for this agreement. As I said at the commencement it is getting stronger, and gaining strength as the days go by. I am not going to quote from this Manitoba paper called the ' Tribune,' but I will ask any hon. gentleman to look at it. It is a Winnipeg paper of some repute, I believe, it is dated the 6th March, 1911, and at page 4 hon. gentlemen from Manitoba who are interested no doubt in what is going on in that province, will see resolutions passed at different points in Manitoba by which the legislature is condemned and in which members are condemned to their faces, being present at these meetings, for the course they have taken and told emphatically that they misrepresented the people of Manitoba when they took the course they did take in supporting the resolution introduced by the premier of that province.
That is the condition there, and in so far as the maritime provinces, Quebec, and I think the most part of Ontario outside of

the centres which are on party grounds against us now we have nothing to fear and everything to hope from this bargain. I have here a paper called ' Farm and Home ' published in Springfield, Massachusetts, and Chicago which has a circulation of over one million copies in the United States, and on its front page is an editorial stating that this agreement is a bad thing for the American farmer and gives the Canadian farmer much the best of it, and certainly if it is a bad thing lor the American farmer according to this newspaper, it must be a good thing for our agricultural community. I now, Sir, have gone over the ground as fully and as rapidly as I could, but I presume my hon. friend (Mr. Bradbury) who follows me will be obliged to take the same course as I did the other night and adjourn the debate. He must excuse me for having taken up so much time, but I can assure my hon. friend that I would like to have concluded at an earlier hour in the evening. I am satisfied, Sir, that upon every ground this is an excellent ap-eement for the people of Canada, that it gives them opportunities which otherwise they could not have, that it is letting us in on the ground floor of the trade of a great country with a population of 100,000,000, a country that every day is needing a greater supply of the products which we can produce, and a country which before many years will possibly be in the same position as England is to-day, importing enormous quantities of food stuffs while exporting none, and devoting itself entirely to its great manufacturing industries. ' If that should come to pass, and if Canada for many years to come will be a produceir of such commodities as will be required for the supply of this industrial nation to the south, is it not well that we should get in now, and hold that market and develop it, rather than that we should let the opportunity slip, and give a chance to other countries to occupy the field against us. We are told that Argentine grows the same kind of natural products as we do, and is our competitor, and is it not in our interest to see that the Argentine Republic does not get a foothold in the United States market ahead of us. Would it not be a good thing for us to hold that market as against all the world? I can see no ground on which we have anything to fear or anything to lose, but I can see on the other hand that we have everything to gain. Then, so far as our loyalty is concerned I hardly think it is worth while discussing it at all. As I pointed out the other evening, where are they going to find the traitors, where are they going to find the man who will not be true to the British flag? We are getting too old in this country to cast off our allegiance; we are proud of our flag, we are proud of the history and tradi-Mr. McKENZIE.
tions of our country, proud of our institutions, proud of being Britishers. What consolation would I or any other Canadian feel in throwing up our caps on the 4th of July? Surely it would take us a long time to get trained to that. We will not try it, and the American people know better than to try to put that yoke over us. We are willing to trade with them, we are willing to develop with them, we are willing to take advantage of the growth and prosperity that would come to us by reason of that trade, but we shall always be true to Canada, true to our own flag, proud of being part and parcel of the greatest empire the world has even seen, an empire on which the sun never sets. I do not think it is worthy of this parliament to discuss such a question as whether or not we will remain true to our own country. We certainly shall. But, while being true to the British Empire we are also as sensible business men bound to take advantage of every trade opportunity that presents itself to make this a great country commercially, and, Sir, as Canada grows in strength, so grows the strength and the standing of the British Empire.
